intro: The first movement, Adagio — Allegro non troppo, of Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74, “Pathétique”, opens with a bassoon at the bottom of its range, and the violins later play a long lyrical melody. In this movement, a passage marked with six pianissimos is followed by an orchestral explosion.

sections.label: Intro · Adagio, bassoon and low strings
sections.mNote: A four-note bassoon phrase rises above the double basses.

sections.label: A · Allegro non troppo, viola theme
sections.mNote: The bassoon’s phrase returns as a quick, detached viola tune.

sections.label: B · D major melody, muted strings
sections.mNote: Muted violins and cellos play the melody in long phrases.

sections.label: Dev · The orchestra breaks in
sections.mNote: The opening tune is pulled apart in racing string passages.

sections.label: B′ · String melody in B major
sections.mNote: The broad string melody returns in the tonic major.

sections.label: Coda · Winds over pizzicato strings, B major
sections.mNote: Descending pizzicato strings accompany the quiet close in B major.

cues.title: Opening, solo bassoon
cues.text: A bassoon begins low, above double basses that descend by semitones. Its four-note phrase rises, is repeated higher, then passes to the violas.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, learning resource on Symphony No. 6, pp. 5–7, with score excerpts of the bassoon, basses and violas. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allegro non troppo, violas
cues.text: The violas take the bassoon’s phrase into the Allegro, adding quick descending notes and playing it short and detached. Second violas and cellos accompany them.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 7: Allegro non troppo, viola theme and accompaniment. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Davydov on the sketches, 1893
cues.text: In February 1893 Tchaikovsky told his nephew Vladimir Davydov that he had finished the sketches for the first movement in less than four days. “You can’t imagine how blissful I feel,” he wrote, “in the conviction that my time is not yet passed, and to work is still possible.”
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4865, 11/23 February 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s composition history. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Second subject, muted strings
cues.text: Muted violins and cellos play the D major melody after the short viola notes. Tchaikovsky marked it teneramente, molto cantabile, con espansione.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 8, reproduces the Andante string theme and its expression markings. The D-major second subject is also identified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Davydov on the programme, 1893
cues.text: In a letter of 11/23 February 1893, Tchaikovsky told Vladimir Davydov that the symphony had a programme which would remain an enigma: “Let them guess.” He also said he had wept while composing it in his head on his travels. The autograph score bears a dedication to Davydov.
cues.evidence: Letter 4865 to Vladimir Davydov, 11/23 February 1893; dedication on the autograph score. Both are documented at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6.

cues.title: Letter to Modest Tchaikovsky, 1893
cues.text: On 3 August 1893, scoring the symphony, Tchaikovsky wrote to his brother Modest: “Today I spent the whole day sitting over two pages — and nothing came out as I wanted it to.” Twenty years earlier he had gone full steam ahead without thinking; now he was timid and unsure of himself.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Modest Tchaikovsky, letter 4984, 22 July/3 August 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s composition history of the symphony. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: End of exposition, bassoon
cues.text: The exposition ends with a bassoon line marked pppppp. The development opens with the full orchestra at fortissimo, and fast strings play fragments of the earlier theme.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10; Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note describes the bassoon’s six-piano marking and the development’s orchestral attack. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Orthodox Requiem quotation, brass
cues.text: In bars 202–205 of the first movement the brass play a fragment of the Orthodox funeral service. Its words ask Christ to give peace to the soul of his servant.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research identifies the Orthodox Requiem quotation in bars 202–205; Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony note identifies its brass scoring. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6 ; https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

cues.title: Balanchine on the first movement
cues.text: George Balanchine, who made a ballet to the symphony’s finale, called this first movement “a blizzard”. In the development, fast strings play fragments of the earlier themes, and the brass, led by trombones and tuba, build the music in wider waves.
cues.evidence: Balanchine’s phrase and his ballet on the fourth movement: Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note. The development’s fast strings and the trombone-and-tuba waves: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10. https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6 ; https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the second subject, B major
cues.text: The broad string melody returns in B major. First heard in D, it now comes back in the major of the symphony’s home key, after the passage for trombones and fast strings.
cues.evidence: The first movement’s B-major second-subject return is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); orchestration and sequence in Queensland Symphony Orchestra’s learning resource, p. 10.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda in B major
cues.text: The closing phrases in the wind and brass sit over descending pizzicato strings. The coda stays in B major to the end of the movement.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10, describes the wind and brass close over descending pizzicato strings. B-major coda: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The title “Pathétique”, 1893
cues.text: Modest Tchaikovsky later claimed that he thought of the title the day after the première. Weeks earlier, on 2 October 1893, the publisher Jurgenson had already written: “What is to be done with pathétique and W. Davidoff or Dawidow?” The dedicatee is Davydov, Tchaikovsky’s nephew.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Symphony No. 6, note 1: Modest’s claim (his 1902 life of his brother, vol. 3, p. 645) set against Jurgenson’s letters to Tchaikovsky of 20 September/2 October and 19/31 October 1893; the title page of the autograph score reads “To Vladimir Lvovich Davydov”. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

transitions.title: Bassoon theme taken over by violas
transitions.from: Intro · Adagio, bassoon and low strings
transitions.to: A · Allegro non troppo, viola theme
transitions.how: At Allegro non troppo the first violas play the bassoon phrase in B minor in a new rhythm, accompanied by the second violas and cellos. Added semiquavers and staccato dots turn the slow solo into a quick string theme.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 5–7, compares the bassoon and viola themes. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

transitions.title: Pause before the D major Andante
transitions.from: A · Allegro non troppo, viola theme
transitions.to: B · D major melody, muted strings
transitions.how: The quick music slows, and an ascending arpeggio passes from cellos to violas. After a pause, muted violins and cellos begin the D major Andante, marked teneramente, molto cantabile, con espansione (tenderly, very singing, with breadth).
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, pp. 7–8; D-major second subject and preceding caesura: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Clarinet solo into the development
transitions.from: B · D major melody, muted strings
transitions.how: A solo clarinet plays a descending line, and its last notes pass to the bassoon, marked pppppp. The full orchestra then enters fortissimo. A half-diminished chord moves the harmony towards D minor, and the strings begin the development.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10; development harmony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: B major after the trombones
transitions.to: B′ · String melody in B major
transitions.how: After the trombones’ climax, phrases in the bass and brass bring the dynamic down. The strings then play the broad Andante tune again in B major, so the D♮ of the home key becomes D♯. The tune moves in long notes, following the semiquavers of the previous passage.
transitions.evidence: First-movement recapitulation and B-major return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10.

transitions.title: B major over pizzicato strings
transitions.from: B′ · String melody in B major
transitions.to: Coda · Winds over pizzicato strings, B major
transitions.how: The returning melody grows quieter. Winds and brass play its last phrases while the strings, playing pizzicato, descend through the close in B major.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 10; the coda’s B major is identified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, I, historical full-score scan
source.locator: PDF pp. 1–3 introduction; p. 12 Andante; pp. 20–43 central argument; pp. 44–51 lyrical return and close. Stage entries summarise broad passages, not every sounding part.

timeline.note: Opening passage: solo bassoon over divided basses; viola joins the low-register texture.
Latter introduction: winds, horns and cellos join the low strings (score PDF p. 2). The report’s change at 0:54 marks this section as a whole, not each entrance.
Allegro section: string figures carry the motif, with replies in the wind and support from the horns.
Andante region: muted violins and cellos share the broad melody; winds and horns support.
Reduced Adagio ending of the exposition: solo clarinet, quiet strings and timpani (score PDF p. 19); the report falls through 8:20–8:50. Placement is approximate.
The exposed bassoon continuation ends the exposition (score PDF p. 19). This brief reduced passage is provisionally placed within the very quiet span at 8:50–8:58 and is not aligned to the bar.
The strings are active throughout the passage, and winds, brass and timpani answer and reinforce them.
Later lyrical return: the broad string line is reinforced by wind and brass.
In the closing passage softer wind harmony and lightly articulated lower strings replace the preceding breadth.

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
